name: Netherlands
tagline: Hundreds of English-taught degrees, and the number is shrinking
summary: The Netherlands is a common choice for IB students in Denmark: hundreds of bachelor's degrees taught entirely in English, three-year programmes, a statutory tuition fee of 2,694 euro for EU students in 2026/27, and a teaching style built on seminars, group work and reading you are expected to do without being chased. Two things have changed. Parliament is working on a law that pushes bachelor's teaching back towards Dutch, and universities have already started cutting or capping English tracks. And the room shortage is genuinely severe - the national student housing monitor published in 2025 estimated a shortage of about 21,500 student rooms in the 19 largest student cities.
whyConsider: Statutory tuition of 2,694 euro for the 2026/27 year applies to you as an EU citizen, at every publicly funded university and hogeschool.
Hundreds of fully English-taught bachelor's degrees, across 13 research universities and a large network of universities of applied sciences.
Research-university bachelor's take three years, like Denmark's; universities of applied sciences take four.
One central portal, Studielink, handles every application to every public institution.
As an EU citizen you can work unlimited hours alongside your studies - no permit, no hour cap.
watchOuts: The Internationalisation in Balance bill (Wet internationalisering in balans, bill 36555) would require bachelor's programmes to be taught mainly in Dutch and force universities to justify every foreign-language programme. On 24 September 2026 it was still before the Tweede Kamer and had not been voted on, but universities are already converting or capping English tracks. Check that the exact programme you want will still run in English in September 2027.

Housing. The national monitor published in 2025 put the shortage at about 21,500 rooms in the 19 largest student cities. Nuffic itself warns of a severe shortage and tells students to start before they arrive. Some universities will not guarantee you a room at all.

Numerus fixus. Popular programmes (medicine, psychology, international business, communication and more) cap places and select. The deadline is 15 January - three and a half months before the normal one, and long before you have IB results.
Numerus fixus programmes can also cap the English-language track separately from the Dutch one, which means the English places can be scarcer than the headline number suggests.

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: 24 points and the award of the full IB Diploma is the floor used across Dutch higher education; individual programmes and numerus fixus selection routinely demand far more. Nuffic does not publish a national minimum score.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: Nuffic compares the full IB Diploma to a Dutch VWO diploma, which is the qualification that gives access to a research university (universiteit) bachelor's. Programmes that require specific school subjects - maths and physics for engineering, maths for economics and econometrics - normally want those subjects at Higher Level, and each university publishes its own HL/SL list. Check the programme page, not a general page.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: There is no national IB-to-Dutch points table. Dutch programmes are either open access (you meet the diploma and subject requirements and you are in) or numerus fixus (the university runs its own selection and sets its own weighting of your grades). Ask the individual programme how it scores IB grades.
notes: IB Course Results / certificates without the full Diploma are not equivalent to VWO and do not give access to a research university bachelor's.
A hogeschool (university of applied sciences) bachelor's needs at least a HAVO-equivalent diploma, so a full IB Diploma comfortably clears that bar and takes four years rather than three.

Because your results arrive on 6 July 2027, you will apply and be admitted conditionally and then send your final IB transcript. Confirm the conditional-offer route with each university - the Dutch system is built around Dutch results arriving in June.

deadlines.label: Studielink opens for the 2027-2028 academic year
deadlines.notes: Published with its year by the University of Amsterdam: "You can submit your enrolment application for the academic year 2027-2028 in Studielink from 1 October 2026 till 15 January 2027." Studielink's information site info.studielink.nl states the 15 January and 1 May deadlines without saying when applications open, so the opening date is taken from the university's page.

deadlines.label: Numerus fixus (selective) programmes
deadlines.notes: Absolute, and published to the minute: Studielink's own guidance is "until 23:59 on 15 January", and the University of Amsterdam states the 2027 date: "from 1 October 2026 till 15 January 2027". You may apply to at most two numerus fixus programmes in one academic year. Medicine, Dentistry, Dental Hygiene and Physiotherapy allow only one application per programme, so you cannot apply for Medicine at two universities. Selection then runs between 15 January and 15 April; what happens on 15 April, and what you then have to do, are entries of their own.

deadlines.label: Numerus fixus ranking numbers issued
deadlines.notes: Published as "Applicants in the selection procedure will receive a ranking number via Studielink on 15 April". Nothing is required of you on the day itself — but this is the day the two-week clock starts for anyone offered a place, so it is the day to start watching Studielink rather than the day to relax. A ranking number above the number of places is not a refusal: places freed by students who do not accept are offered down the list, so ranking 101 of 100 places can still become an offer.

deadlines.label: Accept your numerus fixus place in Studielink
deadlines.notes: The deadline is two weeks from your own offer, not a day in the calendar. Published as "If you are offered a place, you have to accept this place via Studielink within two weeks", and Studielink is explicit that a place not accepted in time "will be assigned to another student automatically". If your offer arrives with the ranking numbers on 15 April, that puts you at the end of April; if it arrives later, because someone above you declined, your fortnight starts then. This is the most expensive thing on the Dutch page to miss and the only one with no date you can set in advance, so the practical answer is to check Studielink from 15 April onwards rather than to wait for an email.

deadlines.label: All other (non-selective) bachelor's programmes
deadlines.year: 2027 entry - Nuffic states the deadline as 1 May; individual universities may set an earlier one
deadlines.notes: Studielink closes at 23:59 on 1 May. The government’s rule is what makes it an equal-consideration date: apply by 1 May and you are entitled to admission to a programme you qualify for ("Aanmelding tot en met 1 mei betekent ook recht op toelating"); a first application after 1 May "kan door de opleiding geweigerd worden" - the programme may still take you, but it does not have to. Some programmes close earlier for capacity or matching reasons, and the programme’s own date is the one that binds.

steps: From autumn 2026, use the Study in NL programme finder to check whether each programme you want is still taught in English for 2027 entry and whether it has a numerus fixus.

Create a Studielink account. With a Dutch address you log in with DigiD; without one you create an account by uploading a scan or photo of your passport or EU identity card, which Studielink verifies automatically. Then add your programme choices.
Apply by 15 January 2027 for any numerus fixus programme, and by 1 May 2027 for open-access programmes.
Complete the university's own application in its student portal: motivation letter, CV, predicted IB grades, transcript, proof of English, sometimes a test or interview.
For open-access programmes, take part in the matching or study check activity - at many universities this is compulsory even though the advice is non-binding.
Numerus fixus results land on 15 April; accept your place within two weeks or it goes to the next person on the list.

Send your final IB transcript as soon as results are released on 6 July 2027 — and ask your IB coordinator to put each university on your transcript list before 5 July, because from that date you request transcripts yourself through rrs.ibo.org at $19 each instead of free through the school. Then enrol, pay the tuition fee, and register with the municipality once you have an address.
application.selectionNotes: Two worlds. Open access: meet the diploma, subject and English requirements and you are admitted, with no competition on grades. Numerus fixus: the programme sets a number of places and runs decentrale selectie, scoring you on grades, motivation, tests, interviews or a written assignment - each programme designs its own procedure and publishes it. Medicine is numerus fixus everywhere and is the hardest route in the country.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Extensive by European standards, but contracting. Study in NL lists the current English-taught offer across all publicly funded institutions; the number of English-taught bachelor's is falling as universities respond to the internationalisation bill, so any count published today may not hold for 2027 entry.
language.englishProof: Universities set their own English requirements. IB English A or English B at Higher Level is commonly accepted as proof, and many programmes waive a test for anyone who completed a fully English-taught secondary education such as the IB Diploma - but this is decided per programme, not nationally. Otherwise the usual bars are IELTS 6.0-6.5 or TOEFL iBT 80-90. Confirm on the programme page before you rely on a waiver.
notes: You will not need Dutch to study or to live in a student city, but you will need it for many part-time jobs outside hospitality and for most internships in Dutch organisations.

The internationalisation bill's core idea is that bachelor's teaching should be predominantly Dutch, with foreign-language programmes allowed only where they can be justified. That is a direct risk to the English-taught offer you are choosing from.

tuitionEuEea.value: 2,694 EUR per year (statutory tuition fee, wettelijk collegegeld)

tuitionNonEu.value: Institutional fee set by each university; Nuffic gives a range of roughly 9,000-20,000 EUR per year for a bachelor's

costs.applicationFee: None for EU/EEA applicants via Studielink. Nuffic notes that some institutions charge non-EEA applicants an application or handling fee of about 75-100 EUR.

livingCostMonthly.value: 1,000-1,500 EUR per month. Nuffic's breakdown (Nibud data, 2024): rent 561, groceries 244, leisure and sport 239, Dutch basic health insurance 133 if you work, transport 67, books and materials 41. Rent alone ranges from about 450 to 1,000 depending on the city.

notes: The statutory fee is set by the government each year and has risen steadily, so budget for a higher figure in 2027/28 than the 2026/27 amount.

You pay the statutory fee only if you hold EU/EEA, Swiss or Surinamese nationality (or a qualifying Dutch residence permit) and do not already hold a degree at that level from a Dutch government-funded institution.

funding.note: The programme must be SU-approved, and outside the Nordics SU is capped at four years (48 klip). Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen before you leave.

funding: Dutch student finance (studiefinanciering) from DUO: open to EU/EEA nationals only in specific cases. Nuffic states plainly that EU students may qualify 'in specific cases' without listing them, and DUO assesses each applicant. Check your own eligibility with DUO directly before counting on it.
Tuition fee loan (collegegeldkrediet) from DUO, for students who are entitled to Dutch student finance.

Institutional scholarships: most universities run a small number of merit scholarships for first-year internationals. They are competitive and rarely cover more than tuition. Search them through the Study in NL Studyfinder.
Part-time work. As an EU citizen you can work without a permit or hour limit, and student jobs in hospitality, supermarkets and university departments are widely available in student cities.
workRights: EU, EEA and Swiss students can work alongside their studies without restrictions - no work permit and no maximum hours (Study in NL / Nuffic, https://www.studyinnl.org/finances/scholarship-and-funding-for-eu-students). Non-EU students need their employer to hold a work permit and are limited to seasonal summer work or a small number of hours per week; check the IND rules before accepting a job.
residency: As an EU citizen you do not need a visa or residence permit. What you do need is a Dutch address and a BSN (citizen service number): register with the gemeente (municipality) of the town you live in shortly after arrival, bringing your passport, your birth certificate and proof of your address. Without a BSN you cannot open most bank accounts, take out insurance or be paid legally. Registration requires a registered address, which is one more reason the housing problem is not just about comfort.
housing: This is the hardest part of studying in the Netherlands and you should plan around it, not hope. The Landelijke Monitor Studentenhuisvesting 2025 (Kences and the Ministry of Housing) estimated a shortage of about 21,500 student rooms in the 19 largest student cities for 2024-25, only slightly down from 22,800 a year earlier. Nuffic describes a 'severe housing shortage' and says there is not enough student accommodation for everyone. Nuffic budgets rent at about 561 EUR a month (Nibud, 2024), more in Amsterdam and Utrecht, less in Enschede, Groningen, Maastricht and Tilburg. Start the search the moment you apply, not when you are admitted. Ask your university's housing office first - some institutions reserve a block of rooms for first-year internationals and those open on a fixed date, often in spring. Use DUWO, Kamernet, Pararius and the university's own listings. Nuffic warns never to sign a contract for a room you have not seen (ask for a video tour) and never to pay brokerage fees, which are not required by law.
healthcare: Bring your blue European Health Insurance Card from the country where you are insured. If you only study, the EHIC plus that coverage is normally enough. The moment you take a paid job or a paid internship in the Netherlands, Dutch law requires you to take out Dutch basic health insurance (basisverzekering) - Nuffic budgets about 133 EUR a month for it. If you are on Dutch basic insurance and on a low income you can usually claim zorgtoeslag (healthcare allowance) from the tax office, which refunds part of the premium. Register with a local GP (huisarts) early; in student cities the good practices fill up.

institutions.name: University of Amsterdam
institutions.note: The largest research university in the country and the most competitive city to find a room in; several of its English bachelor's are numerus fixus.

institutions.name: Delft University of Technology
institutions.note: The strongest engineering school in the Netherlands; its English-taught bachelor's expect HL Mathematics and HL Physics and several carry a numerus fixus.

institutions.name: Maastricht University
institutions.note: The most international university in the country and built entirely on problem-based learning in small tutorial groups, which suits students coming out of IB seminars.

institutions.name: University of Groningen
institutions.note: A big, old research university in a city where students are close to half the population, and one of the cheaper places to rent.

institutions.name: Utrecht University
institutions.note: A large, broad research university in a lively student city, with University College Utrecht, its residential liberal-arts college, on its campus.

institutions.name: Leiden University
institutions.note: The oldest Dutch university, with a second campus in The Hague built around international law, security and governance.

institutions.name: Erasmus University Rotterdam
institutions.note: The business and economics powerhouse; Rotterdam School of Management's International Business Administration takes 650 students a year and is selective.

institutions.name: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
institutions.note: Amsterdam's second research university, smaller and less frantic than UvA, with a strong PPE and AI offer.

institutions.name: Eindhoven University of Technology
institutions.note: All bachelor's are taught in English and the university sits inside the Brainport tech cluster, so internships with ASML and Philips are normal.

institutions.name: University of Twente
institutions.note: It calls itself the only campus university in the Netherlands, with more than 3,000 student rooms on site - which matters a lot given the national room shortage.

institutions.name: Wageningen University & Research
institutions.note: Specialised in agriculture, food, nature and the environment, in a small town built around the university.

institutions.name: Radboud University
institutions.note: A green campus university in a mid-sized city, strong in cognitive science and neuroscience, with a calmer housing market than the Randstad.

institutions.name: Tilburg University
institutions.note: Small and focused on social sciences, economics and law, with its numerus fixus selection criteria published in detail.

institutions.name: Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences
institutions.note: Four-year, practice-led degrees with compulsory internships - a different and often underrated route for IB students who want work experience built into the degree.

institutions.name: Breda University of Applied Sciences
institutions.note: Small and specialised, with English-taught bachelor's in games, creative media, data science and AI, leisure, tourism and hotel management.

institutions.name: Hanze University of Applied Sciences
institutions.note: A large applied-sciences school in a cheap, very student-heavy city, with an unusually strong conservatoire attached.

institutions.name: The Hague University of Applied Sciences
institutions.englishBachelors: About 17 English-taught bachelor's, including International Business, European Studies, International and European Law and Applied Computer Science
institutions.note: A large hogeschool in The Hague, the city of international courts and organisations, with about 17 bachelor's degrees taught in English.

institutions.name: Amsterdam University College
institutions.englishBachelors: One three-year Bachelor of Arts and Sciences in liberal arts and sciences, taught entirely in English
institutions.note: A small, selective liberal-arts college run jointly by the University of Amsterdam and VU Amsterdam, where first-years live on campus.

institutions.name: University College Utrecht
institutions.englishBachelors: One three-year liberal arts and sciences bachelor, taught entirely in English
institutions.note: Utrecht University's residential liberal-arts college, where you design your own major; it selects on more than grades.

institutions.name: Rotterdam University of Applied Sciences
institutions.englishBachelors: Three English-taught bachelor's: International Business, and Fine Art and Graphic Design at Willem de Kooning Academy
institutions.note: A very large hogeschool that now teaches only three bachelor's in English, so check your programme is one of them.

institutions.name: Fontys University of Applied Sciences
institutions.englishBachelors: English-taught bachelor's in engineering, ICT, business and the performing arts, spread over Eindhoven, Venlo and Tilburg
institutions.note: A large hogeschool with campuses in Eindhoven, Tilburg and Venlo; check which city your English-taught programme is in.

institutions.name: University College Roosevelt
institutions.englishBachelors: One three-year liberal arts and sciences bachelor, taught entirely in English
institutions.note: A small residential liberal-arts college of Utrecht University, in the provincial town of Middelburg in Zeeland.
